sections.title: Sec 1: Atomic Structure & Valence Electrons
lecture_lines: Atoms have a nucleus and shells.
Outermost layer is the valence shell.
Stability means a full outer shell.
animations: Animation step 1: Fade in a central yellow circle (nucleus) labeled 'Nucleus'. Three concentric light gray circles (#CCCCCC) appear around it, labeled 'Shell 1', 'Shell 2', 'Shell 3'.
Animation step 2: Highlight the outermost circle with a pulsing bright white (#FFFFFF) stroke. Label it 'Valence Shell' in bright white text next to it.
Animation step 3: Display text 'Octet Rule: Full Outer Shell' at the top. Animate a generic atom filling its outer shell to 8 electrons, turning green (#00FF00) to indicate stability.
Animation step 4: Show Sodium (Na) model: 11 protons in nucleus. 2 electrons in Shell 1, 8 in Shell 2, 1 in Shell 3. The single outer electron glows bright red (#FF0000).

Animation step 5: Show Chlorine (Cl) model: 17 protons in nucleus. 2 electrons in Shell 1, 8 in Shell 2, 7 in Shell 3. Highlight the empty spot in Shell 3 with a dashed white circle labeled 'Missing 1'.

sections.title: Sec 2: The Transfer: Sodium Gives, Chlorine Takes
animations: Animation step 1: Display Na (left) and Cl (right) side-by-side. The single red electron on Na's outer shell pulses intensely, preparing to detach.
Animation step 2: The red electron detaches from Na and moves horizontally across the gap to Cl's outer shell, filling the missing spot.
Animation step 3: As the electron moves, a trail of red particles follows it, emphasizing the physical transfer of charge.
Animation step 4: The Na atom shrinks slightly (scale 0.9) and its nucleus glows bright red (#FF0000). A large red '+' sign appears above it.
Animation step 5: The Cl atom expands slightly (scale 1.1) and its nucleus glows bright blue (#0000FF). A large blue '-' sign appears above it.

sections.title: Sec 3: Ion Formation: Charge and Identity
animations: Animation step 1: Split the screen vertically. Left side shows Na, right side shows Cl. A digital counter box appears above each.
Animation step 2: On the left, the counter updates to '11 Protons' (red) and '10 Electrons' (blue). A large red '+' sign flashes next to Na.
Animation step 3: On the right, the counter updates to '17 Protons' (red) and '18 Electrons' (blue). A large blue '-' sign flashes next to Cl.
Animation step 4: A balance scale icon appears. On the Na side, the 'Proton' weight is heavier, tipping the scale, labeled 'Positive Charge'.
Animation step 5: On the Cl side, the 'Electron' weight is heavier, tipping the scale opposite, labeled 'Negative Charge'. Text 'Na+' and 'Cl-' appear below each atom.

sections.title: Sec 4: Electrostatic Attraction: The Ionic Bond
lecture_lines: Ions pull into a stable bond.
This connection is the ionic bond.
animations: Animation step 1: The Na+ (red glow) and Cl- (blue glow) ions start at opposite edges of the screen.
Animation step 2: The ions accelerate towards each other. Glowing yellow (#FFFF00) lines appear between them, representing force fields.
Animation step 3: The ions collide softly and lock together. The yellow lines solidify into a rigid, glowing bridge between the nuclei.
Animation step 4: Text 'Not Shared Electrons' appears with a red cross mark. Text 'Electrostatic Pull' appears with a green check mark.
Animation step 5: A label 'Ionic Bond' fades in above the connected ions, with an arrow pointing to the glowing bridge.

sections.title: Sec 5: The Result: The Crystal Lattice of NaCl
animations: Animation step 1: The central Na+-Cl- pair remains. New Na+ (red) and Cl- (blue) ions fly in from all four corners.
Animation step 2: The ions arrange themselves into a 2D checkerboard pattern, alternating red and blue squares.
Animation step 3: The camera zooms out slightly. More layers of ions appear above and below, suggesting a 3D cube structure.
Animation step 4: The grid solidifies into a white, crystalline cube shape. Label 'Crystal Lattice' appears next to it.
Animation step 5: The cube transforms into a simple cartoon salt shaker. Text 'Sodium Chloride (NaCl)' appears below. The shaker shakes its head 'no' to liquid, indicating solid state.
